blocks.content: 1.1 Ancient History of Madhya Pradesh

Madhya Pradesh has one of the richest archaeological and historical legacies in India. The region has been inhabited since the Stone Age, with evidence of prehistoric settlements discovered at various sites across the state. Rock paintings at Bhimbetka, located near Bhopal, are among the oldest known rock art in the world, dating back to over 30,000 years ago. These paintings were discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957-58 and were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.

The ancient name of the central Indian region was 'Avanti,' and its capital was Ujjain (ancient Ujjayini). Ujjain was one of the seven sacred cities of Hinduism and was a major center of trade, learning, and culture in ancient India. It served as the capital of the Avanti Mahajanapada, which was one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas mentioned in ancient Buddhist texts.
Prehistoric Era

items: Bhimbetka Rock Shelters - UNESCO World Heritage Site, over 700 rock shelters, oldest evidence of human habitation in India
Adamgarh Hills (Hoshangabad) - Another significant prehistoric site with rock paintings
Raisen District - Contains numerous Mesolithic and Neolithic sites
Pachmarhi - Rock paintings and cave settlements from prehistoric periods

blocks.content: Vedic and Mahajanapada Period

During the Vedic period, the central Indian region was known as part of the Madhyadesa, the 'Middle Country.' The region of present-day Madhya Pradesh comprised several ancient kingdoms. The Avanti Mahajanapada with its capital at Ujjain was the most prominent. Other kingdoms included Chedi (with capital at Shuktimati, present-day Banda area), and parts of the Matsya and Kuru kingdoms in the northern areas.
Mauryan Period

The Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya (321-297 BCE) incorporated the entire region of present-day Madhya Pradesh. Emperor Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta, served as the Viceroy of Ujjain before ascending to the throne. Ashoka built the famous Sanchi Stupa near present-day Vidisha district. The Sanchi complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and represents one of the finest examples of early Buddhist architecture in India.

The Ashokan edicts at Sanchi, Rupnath (Jabalpur district), Saro-Maro (Shahdol), and Panguraria (Sehore) provide invaluable historical information about the Mauryan administration and society. Vidisha (ancient Besnagar) was an important administrative center and commercial hub during the Mauryan period.
Post-Mauryan Period – Sungas, Kushanas and Satavahanas

After the decline of the Mauryan Empire, the Shunga dynasty rose to power under Pushyamitra Shunga (185-149 BCE). The Shungas were great patrons of Hindu culture and art. They expanded the Sanchi Stupa and added magnificent gateways (toranas). The Shunga Empire had its capital at Pataliputra but controlled most of central India. Vidisha was an important city during this period.

The Western Kshatrapas (Sakas) ruled over western Madhya Pradesh, particularly Ujjain, from around 35 CE to 405 CE. The most famous king of this dynasty was Rudradaman I (130-150 CE) who left behind the Junagarh rock inscription. The Satavahanas controlled parts of southern Madhya Pradesh during this period.
Gupta Empire

The Gupta Empire (320-550 CE) ushered in what is called the 'Golden Age' of Indian history. Madhya Pradesh was at the heart of the Gupta Empire, with important centers at Pataliputra, Vidisha, Ujjain, and Eran. The Gupta rulers were great patrons of art, literature, science, and religion. Chandragupta II (375-415 CE), also known as Vikramaditya, made Ujjain his western capital. The famous Navratnas (nine gems) of his court included the poet Kalidasa, astronomer Aryabhata, and physician Dhanvantari.

items: Eran (Sagar district) - Important Gupta center with famous Iron Pillar and Varaha sculpture
Udayagiri Caves (Vidisha) - 20 rock-cut caves from Gupta period with famous Varaha Avatar panel
Deogarh (Lalitpur, now UP border) - Dashavatara Temple from Gupta period
Besnagar (Vidisha) - Important Gupta administrative and religious center

blocks.content: Paramara Dynasty and Medieval Period

The Paramara dynasty ruled the Malwa region (western MP) from 9th to 14th century CE with capital at Dhar. The most celebrated Paramara ruler was Raja Bhoja (1010-1055 CE), one of the greatest scholar-kings in Indian history. He established the renowned Bhoj Shala at Dhar, which served as a center of Sanskrit learning. He wrote numerous texts on architecture, poetry, grammar, and statecraft. Bhopal's famous upper lake (Bada Talab) is traditionally attributed to Raja Bhoja.

The Chandela dynasty controlled the Bundelkhand region (eastern MP) from 9th to 12th centuries. They built the magnificent Khajuraho temples, which are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. These temples were built between 950-1050 CE and represent the pinnacle of Nagara style architecture. The Chandela capital was at Mahoba and Kalinjar.
1.2 Medieval History of Madhya Pradesh
Delhi Sultanate Period

The Delhi Sultanate extended its authority over Madhya Pradesh gradually from the 13th century. Iltutmish captured Gwalior in 1232 CE. The region saw several changes in control as different Sultanate dynasties rose and fell. The Khalji and Tughlaq rulers made periodic expeditions into the Deccan passing through Madhya Pradesh. Alauddin Khalji's campaigns into the Deccan in the early 14th century significantly impacted the region.

The Tomar Rajputs ruled the Gwalior region as vassals of the Delhi Sultans and later became independent. Man Singh Tomar (1486-1516 CE) was the greatest Tomar ruler who built the famous Man Mandir Palace in Gwalior Fort. He was also a great patron of music and is associated with the Dhrupad style of classical music. The Gwalior Fort, which Raja Mansingh developed extensively, is one of the finest medieval forts in India.
Malwa Sultanate

The Malwa Sultanate was established in 1401 CE after Dilawar Khan Ghuri declared independence from the Delhi Sultanate. The Malwa Sultanate had its capital at Mandu (Mandavgadh), which became one of the most spectacular fortified cities in medieval India. The Ghuri dynasty was succeeded by the Khalji dynasty of Malwa under Mahmud Khalji (1436-1469 CE).

Mandu (Mandav) flourished as the capital of the Malwa Sultanate. Important monuments built here include the Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal, Hoshang Shah's Tomb (first marble building in India), Jami Mosque, and the romantic Baz Bahadur's Palace associated with the love story of Baz Bahadur and Rani Roopmati.
Sur Dynasty and Akbar's Conquest

Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun and became Emperor of India (1540-1545 CE). He built the famous Grand Trunk Road passing through parts of northern MP. After Akbar regained the throne, the Mughal Empire gradually incorporated Madhya Pradesh. Akbar defeated Baz Bahadur of Malwa in 1561 CE and incorporated Malwa into the Mughal Empire. He also captured the Gwalior Fort.
Bundela Rajputs

The Bundela Rajputs were among the most powerful dynasties in Madhya Pradesh during the 17th-18th centuries. Chhatrasal Bundela (1649-1731 CE) was the greatest Bundela hero who fought for independence from the Mughals. After the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the Marathas emerged as the dominant power in central India.

items: Orchha - Important Bundela capital with magnificent Raj Mahal, Jahangir Mahal, and Chaturbhuj Temple
Datia - Another significant Bundela center with Datia Palace
Chhatarpur - Named after Chhatrasal, important Bundela center

blocks.content: 1.3 Maratha Rule in Madhya Pradesh

After the decline of the Mughal Empire, the Marathas rapidly expanded into Madhya Pradesh. Three major Maratha dynasties established themselves in the region: the Holkars of Indore, the Scindias (Shinde) of Gwalior, and the Pawars of Dewas-Dhar. The Peshwa-controlled territories also included parts of Madhya Pradesh.

Ahilyabai Holkar (1725-1795 CE) was one of the greatest rulers of Indore. She was the daughter-in-law of Malhar Rao Holkar. After her husband Khanderao and father-in-law Malhar Rao died, she became the regent and later ruler of Indore. She was known for her justice, religious tolerance, and massive construction activities across India. She built or restored temples, ghats, dharamshalas, and wells across the subcontinent. Her capital was Maheshwar on the Narmada.
1.4 British Period in Madhya Pradesh

The British East India Company gradually extended its control over central India through the early 19th century. After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18), the British established control over the major princely states of the region. The Central Provinces were formally organized as a British administrative unit, with Nagpur as the headquarters.
Central Provinces and Central India Agency

The British organized the region into the Central Provinces (CP) and Berar, and the Central India Agency. The Central Provinces were formally constituted in 1861 and included Nagpur Division and parts of the Narmada Valley. Berar was added to CP in 1903. The Central India Agency comprised numerous princely states including Gwalior, Indore, Bhopal, and several smaller states. Nagpur was the capital of Central Provinces.
Freedom Struggle in MP

Madhya Pradesh played a significant role in India's freedom struggle. The 1857 Revolt (First War of Independence) had significant manifestations in the region. Major centers of the 1857 uprising in present-day MP included:

items: Jhansi - Led by Rani Lakshmibai (though Jhansi is now in UP, the battle extended to MP territory)
Gwalior - Battle of Gwalior where Rani Lakshmibai fell on June 18, 1858
Sagar - Important military center during 1857 revolt
Mandla - Tribal uprising under Shankar Shah and his son Raghunath Shah
Indore - Mutiny at the Holkar forces

blocks.content: During the Indian National Congress-led freedom movement, many prominent leaders from MP participated actively. Shankar Dayal Sharma, B.R. Ambedkar, and many others had connections to the region. The Non-Cooperation Movement, Civil Disobedience Movement, and Quit India Movement all had active participation from the people of Madhya Pradesh.
1.5 Formation of Madhya Pradesh

After India's independence in 1947, the States Reorganisation Commission was set up under Justice Fazal Ali in 1953. Based on its recommendations, the States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956. On November 1, 1956, the state of Madhya Pradesh was formed by merging the former Central Provinces and Berar, the former princely states of Madhya Bharat (including Gwalior and Indore), Vindhya Pradesh, and Bhopal State.

Bhopal became the capital of the new Madhya Pradesh state. In 2000, on November 1, the Chhattisgarh State was carved out of the southeastern districts of Madhya Pradesh. The new MP, after bifurcation, still remained the second-largest state in India in terms of area.
